issues.legal_issue: Royalty payable for minerals extracted under a mining lease is included in the annual rent value used to calculate land cess.
material_facts: The land was occupied under a mining lease permitting extraction of iron ore.
The lease required payment of surface rent, dead rent, and royalty on extracted ore.
The cess demand included the royalty payable under the lease in calculating annual rent value.
issues.conclusion: Royalty payable for minerals won from the land is distinct from payment for use of the land surface and is included in annual rent value for land-cess calculation.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 78 and 79(1) of the Madras District Boards Act, the annual rent value for leased land includes the lease amount and royalty payable to the government. The expression royalty, following lease amount, refers to payment for materials or minerals won from the land, rather than payment for use of its surface.

rule.if: land_cess_demand_challenge and land_occupied_under_mining_lease and lease_requires_mineral_royalty and royalty_included_in_rent_value_calculation

predicates.land_cess_demand_challenge: A person challenges a demand to pay cess assessed on occupied land.
predicates.land_occupied_under_mining_lease: The land is occupied under a lease permitting the extraction of minerals.
predicates.lease_requires_mineral_royalty: The lease requires payment calculated by reference to minerals extracted from the land.
predicates.royalty_included_in_rent_value_calculati: The authority includes the mineral-related payment in calculating the land's annual rent value.

issues.definition: When a land-cess demand concerns land occupied under a mining lease that requires mineral-related payments, those payments are included in annual rent value if the authority has included them in its calculation.

issues.legal_issue: Central legislation regulating mine and mineral development does not impliedly repeal a land-cess levy that serves a separate purpose and does not regulate or develop mines and minerals.
material_facts: The cess was imposed on occupied land and its proceeds were credited to a district fund for local administration and public amenities.
The central enactments concerned regulation and development of mines and minerals.
The land-cess provisions did not concern the development or regulation of mines and minerals.
issues.conclusion: The central enactments did not repeal or displace the land-cess provisions because the levy and the central regulation of mines and minerals did not overlap in purpose or field.
issues.legal_principle: The Court distinguished Hingir Rampur Coal Co. v. State of Orissa, [1961] 2 S.C.R. 537, and State of Orissa v. M. A. Tullock & Co., A.I.R. 1964 S.C. 1284. Those cases concerned a state enactment for development of mining areas that overlapped with central mine-and-mineral legislation. The land-cess provisions instead served local administration and were unrelated to mine development or regulation; therefore, there was no overlapping field requiring implied repeal.

rule.if: challenge_to_land_cess_demand and cess_funds_local_administration and central_law_regulates_mines_or_minerals and cess_provision_does_not_regulate_mines_or_minerals

predicates.challenge_to_land_cess_demand: A person challenges a demand for a cess imposed on occupied land.
predicates.cess_funds_local_administration: The proceeds of the cess are used for local administration or public amenities.
predicates.central_law_regulates_mines_or_minerals: A central enactment regulates or develops mines or minerals.
predicates.cess_provision_does_not_regulate_mines_o: The provision imposing the cess does not regulate mines or minerals.

issues.definition: A land-cess provision serving local administration is not displaced by central mine-and-mineral legislation when the cess provision does not regulate mines or minerals.

issues.legal_issue: A cess calculated by reference to the annual rent value of occupied land is a tax on land, not a tax on mineral rights, even when the rent value includes royalty under a mining lease.
material_facts: The cess was imposed on occupied land, and its basis was the land's annual rent value.
For leased land, the statutory calculation used the amount payable for the lease, including surface rent, dead rent, and royalty under the mining lease.
The royalty was connected to the minerals extracted, but the cess was assessed by reference to the rent value of the land.
issues.conclusion: The land cess was in substance a tax on land within Entry 49 of the State List, not a tax on mineral rights within Entry 50.
issues.legal_principle: The true nature of a taxing statute is determined by examining its substance. Sections 78 and 79 of the Madras District Boards Act imposed a cess on occupied land using annual rent value as its basis; for leased land, that value reflected the amount paid for the property. The Court accordingly treated the levy as a tax on lands under Entry 49 of the State List, rather than a tax on mineral rights under Entry 50.

predicates.challenge_to_land_cess_demand: A person challenges a demand for a cess imposed on occupied land.
predicates.cess_based_on_occupied_land_rent_value: The cess is calculated by reference to the annual rent value of occupied land.
predicates.mining_lease_payments_form_part_of_rent_: Payments due under a mining lease, including payments connected to mineral extraction, form part of the rent value used for the cess.

issues.definition: When a cess is assessed on occupied land by reference to its annual rent value, including payments due under a mining lease, the levy is a tax on land rather than on mineral rights.

issues.legal_issue: A lawfully imposed cess on land may be recovered as an arrear of land revenue under the general revenue-recovery law even if the tax-recovery provision in the land-cess statute does not apply.
material_facts: The demands sought recovery of a cess imposed on land as arrears of land revenue.
The Court accepted that the provision in the District Boards Act for recovery of sums due as taxes did not apply to this recovery.
The cess was not disputed to be a cess lawfully imposed upon land.
The Revenue Recovery Act authorized recovery as arrears of land revenue of cesses lawfully imposed upon land.
issues.conclusion: The proposed recovery procedure was lawful under section 52 of the Madras Revenue Recovery Act, notwithstanding the inapplicability of section 221 of the Madras District Boards Act.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Madras Revenue Recovery Act authorizes recovery as arrears of land revenue of cesses lawfully imposed upon land, unless another recovery procedure is specially provided. Section 221 of the Madras District Boards Act did not apply to the recovery at issue, but its inapplicability did not prevent use of section 52.

predicates.recovery_as_land_revenue_sought: The authority seeks to recover the cess as an arrear of land revenue.
predicates.cess_lawfully_imposed_on_land: The cess was lawfully imposed upon land.
predicates.no_special_recovery_procedure_applies: No specially provided recovery procedure governs the recovery at issue.

issues.definition: A lawfully imposed cess on land is recoverable as an arrear of land revenue when recovery is sought that way and no specially provided recovery procedure applies.
